bugs: The mail is sent synchronously inside a DB::afterCommit callback (app/Models/Order.php:58). If the mailer throws after the top-level commit, the order is already shipped and the points are already added, but the API returns 500. A retry then gets 409, so the email is lost. A probe with a throwing Mail confirmed the status was 'shipped', the points were 5, and the exception surfaced.

ShipOrderRequest::authorize() returns `$this->user()->is_staff` with no cast (app/Http/Requests/ShipOrderRequest.php:11). UserFactory doesn't set is_staff, so an in-memory factory user acting via Sanctum::actingAs gives null, which causes a TypeError and a 500 instead of 403. A probe confirmed this. In production the user is loaded from the DB, so it is test-fragile rather than live.
antipatterns: Authorization lives in FormRequest::authorize() rather than a Policy or Gate with ->can() on the route (app/Http/Requests/ShipOrderRequest.php:9-12, routes/api.php:11-12). It works, but it isn't reusable for back-office callers.
Synchronous Mail::send in a request path instead of a queued mailable (app/Models/Order.php:58)

The rollback test calls DB::rollBack() manually inside DB::transaction() instead of throwing (tests/Feature/ShipOrderTest.php:128-131). That isn't a realistic back-office failure, and it confuses the transaction level.
Order::customer() relation instead of the conventional user() (app/Models/Order.php:28-31). This is defensible, but it forces `for($customer, 'customer')` everywhere.
UserFactory doesn't define the is_staff or points defaults (database/factories/UserFactory.php)
strengths: An atomic conditional UPDATE claims the order, which prevents a double ship under concurrent requests, and the unique order_id is a backstop
DB::afterCommit defers the mail, so it isn't sent on rollback. The points increment sits inside the same transaction, so it rolls back with it
The mail stays easy to test with Mail::fake: assertNothingSent holds inside the open outer transaction and assertSentCount(1) holds after commit
Markdown mailable with a test of the rendered content (assertSeeInHtml / assertSeeInText)
Good test coverage: a repeated ship, a DB uniqueness constraint, a pending order shipping, the rounding dataset, and outer commit vs rollback

bugs: Mail::fake() ignores ->afterCommit() on queued mailables. A probe with Mail::fake plus an outer rollback still saw OrderShipped queued (app/Models/Order.php:58). Production behaviour is correct, but the rollback guarantee can't be checked with the standard fake. The suite works around this by asserting on the array transport (tests/Feature/ShipOrderTest.php:12-15, 133-149).
antipatterns: The tests read Mail::mailer('array')->getSymfonyTransport()->messages() directly instead of using Mail::fake assertions in most cases (tests/Feature/ShipOrderTest.php:12-15, 42). This is low-level, and it's needed only because of the afterCommit/fake gap above.
The comment on app/Models/Order.php:57 restates what ->afterCommit() already says
The controller passes double-quoted string literals to validated() (app/Http/Controllers/ShipOrderController.php:13). This is a small style inconsistency.
strengths: Uses an OrderPolicy plus ->can('ship', 'order') route middleware, so 403 is returned before validation runs. Authorization is reusable and kept out of the FormRequest.

An atomic conditional UPDATE claims the order, so concurrent requests can't double-ship and a 409 does nothing again. Probes confirmed that a stale second instance also gets 409 and points are added only once.

A queued mailable (ShouldQueue) with ->afterCommit(): with the database queue, a probe showed no job row after an outer rollback and exactly one after commit. Sending is off the request path, so a mail failure can't cause a 500 after commit.
Points are incremented in SQL inside the same transaction, so they roll back with the outer transaction
Clean modern Laravel: #[Fillable] attributes, a casts() method, an enum-cast status, a factory state for staff, and is_staff/points defaults in UserFactory

Tests cover the rounding dataset including zero, adding to an existing balance, guest/non-staff/404/409, a validation dataset with messages, and outer rollback and commit with real assertions on the order, shipment, points and mail

v.rationale: Both implementations use the same core design: a transaction, an atomic conditional UPDATE to claim the order, an SQL increment for points, a deferred email, and a unique order_id. Both pass their suites (impl-2: 19 tests, impl-1: 18 tests). impl-2 ranks first. It uses a Policy with route ->can() for authorization and a queued, afterCommit mailable, so the email is never sent on rollback and a mail failure can't cause a 500 after the order is already shipped. Its UserFactory also defines the new column defaults. Its one weakness is testability: Mail::fake doesn't honor afterCommit, so the suite falls back to inspecting the array transport. impl-1 sends the mail synchronously in DB::afterCommit. A probe confirmed that a mailer failure after commit returns 500 even though the order is shipped and the points are added, so a retry gets 409 and the email is lost. Its FormRequest authorize() returns the raw is_staff attribute, which gave a 500 in a probe with an in-memory factory user. On the plus side, impl-1's mail is easier to test with Mail::fake, and it includes a mail-content test and a DB-uniqueness test. Its rollback test uses an unrealistic manual DB::rollBack().
